cues.text: Welcome to P Block Chemistry.
This recorded class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
The p block spans groups thirteen to eighteen.
In the usual main group pattern, the outer s subshell contains two electrons,
while the outer p subshell contains one through six.
Three outer electrons correspond to group thirteen, and eight correspond to
group eighteen.
Helium is the important exception: its filled first shell has only two
electrons, yet its chemical behaviour places it with the noble gases.
An outer three s two, three p three configuration belongs to period three and
group fifteen.
The period identifies the outer principal shell, while the group reflects the
main group valence pattern.
Across a typical period, increasing effective nuclear attraction generally
reduces radius and increases nonmetallic character.
Down a group, additional occupied shells generally increase size and metallic
character.
These are starting trends rather than complete predictions of every property.
Before comparing melting points, distinguish molecular substances,
metallic structures and extended networks; they need not follow the same
smooth
pattern.
The first p block members differ from heavier members for structural reasons.
Boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine have small second period valence
shells.
Their size, electronegativity and orbital overlap affect which bonds and
structures are favoured.
They cannot be treated as if their valence shells expand arbitrarily to
imitate
every heavier congener.
Saying anomalous is only a label; a useful explanation identifies the bonding
or electronic cause.
Among several heavier groups, a lower oxidation state becomes more important
relative to the group maximum.
This is commonly discussed through the inert pair effect.
Thallium plus one and lead plus two are examples of lower states becoming
relatively stable.
It does not mean higher oxidation states never occur, or that the outer s
electrons are unavailable in every compound.
Oxidation state stability depends on the actual ligands, bonding and reaction
environment.
A group number identifies possible electron bookkeeping patterns, but cannot
by
itself establish which compound is most stable.
Compare specified species rather than treating the trend as an absolute
prohibition.
Group thirteen commonly shows oxidation state plus three, while plus one
becomes important for some heavier members.
Boron is a nonmetal and often forms covalent, electron deficient structures.
Aluminium has stronger metallic character.
Boron trifluoride is a useful Lewis acid example: it can accept an electron
pair from a suitable donor.
Do not rank all Lewis acids from one octet drawing alone, because bonding
interactions and the reacting partner matter.
Group fourteen includes carbon and silicon together with more metallic heavier
elements.
Carbon forms strong carbon carbon bonds, supporting extensive catenation and
many stable multiple bonds.
Silicon's larger orbitals and different overlap lead to different structures.
Carbon dioxide consists of discrete molecules, while common solid silicon
dioxide is an extended network of silicon oxygen bonds.
A formula ratio of one central atom to two oxygens therefore does not imply
identical physical properties.
Plus four and plus two states also change in relative importance down group
fourteen.
Use the group pattern to organize a comparison, then inspect the actual
bonding
and structure.
Group fifteen has two outer s electrons and three outer p electrons.
Common oxidation states include minus three, plus three and plus five,
depending on the atoms bonded to the element.
Nitrogen's strong nitrogen nitrogen triple bond helps explain the relatively
low reactivity of molecular nitrogen under ordinary conditions.
That statement concerns the molecule, not a claim that every nitrogen compound
is unreactive.
Nitrogen also cannot simply imitate every five coordinate structure of a
heavier group member.
For the common hydride comparison, ammonia is more basic than the heavier
hydrides in the usual introductory sequence.
Thermal stability also generally decreases down that series.
Ammonia's intermolecular hydrogen bonding makes its boiling behaviour unusual
compared with a simple increase based only
on molar mass.
Basicity, thermal stability and boiling point are different properties: one
ordering must not be copied automatically into another column.
State which compounds are being compared and what conditions apply.
A lone pair may be present in several hydrides while its availability and the
stability of the protonated product still differ.
Group sixteen has six outer electrons in the usual main group pattern.
Oxygen commonly has oxidation number minus two, but that value is not
universal.
Peroxides, superoxides and oxygen fluorine compounds require different
assignments.
Sulfur and heavier members can also have positive oxidation states in suitable
compounds.
Write the actual formula and apply charge balance instead of turning group
membership into a fixed ionic charge.
Water has unusually strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding compared with
nearby
heavier group sixteen hydrides.
Its boiling point therefore departs from a simple mass based comparison.
In the elementary hydride series, acidity generally increases toward heavier
members as the element hydrogen bond becomes easier to break, while thermal
stability decreases.
Acidity concerns proton transfer under specified conditions; boiling concerns
separation of molecules into vapour.
These processes should not be treated as one trend.
In a ranking problem, identify the property before applying an arrow down the
periodic table.
Later worked examples will use peroxide, superoxide and oxygen difluoride to
check oxygen bookkeeping directly.
Group seventeen has seven outer electrons and commonly forms compounds in
which
the halogen has oxidation number minus one.
Fluorine is assigned minus one in its compounds, while heavier halogens can
have positive oxidation states when bonded to more electronegative partners.
Near room temperature, fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid
and
iodine is a solid.
Increasing polarizability strengthens dispersion attractions down the
molecular
series.
Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine, yet chlorine has a more
negative first electron gain enthalpy.
An incoming electron encounters stronger repulsion in fluorine's compact
shell,
producing this familiar exception.
Aqueous oxidizing strength involves several energy changes, so electron gain
enthalpy alone cannot determine the complete ranking.
Fluorine remains a very strong oxidizing agent in ordinary aqueous
comparisons.
Hydrogen fluoride is a weak acid in dilute water compared with the usual
strong
hydrogen chloride, bromide and iodide acids.
Its strong bond and the solution environment matter.
Keep these different properties and their definitions in separate columns when
explaining halogen trends.
Noble gases have filled valence shells, making many ordinary reactions
unfavourable.
Their atoms are normally monatomic rather than joined into the familiar
diatomic molecules of halogens.
Weak dispersion attractions help explain their low boiling temperatures.
Down the group, increasing polarizability generally raises boiling points,
while the outer electrons become easier to remove.
A filled shell therefore does not give identical physical properties to every
member.
Heavier noble gases can form compounds under suitable conditions.
Xenon compounds with strongly electronegative partners show why inert is a
contextual description rather than a rule forbidding all bonding.
Helium's very small filled first shell is particularly resistant to ordinary
chemical bonding and is a distinctive first member.
Do not infer that a helium configuration requires six p electrons: helium has
a
filled first s subshell.
When comparing reactivity, identify the species and conditions instead of
assigning every group eighteen atom an absolute inability to react.
Physical trends and exceptional chemical compounds provide complementary
evidence about the same group.
A reliable comparison starts by naming the property.
Radius, ionization energy, acidity, boiling point and oxidation state
stability
describe different processes.
Next identify whether the objects are elements, ions or compounds, and whether
the change is across a period or down a group.
Only then apply the relevant broad trend.
Carbon dioxide compared with silicon dioxide is mainly a bonding and structure
comparison.
Ammonia and water highlight intermolecular hydrogen bonding.
Chlorine compared with fluorine highlights the difference between electron
gain
and electronegativity.
These examples do not justify applying one exception to every unrelated
property.
If a numerical table is supplied, read its units, temperature, pressure and
radius or energy convention.
The data are evidence to interpret, rather than an inconvenience to replace
with a memorized slogan.
In a written explanation, connect the observation with shell size, shielding,
orbital overlap or intermolecular attraction as appropriate.
Finally check the first member and any unusual structure before deciding
whether the broad ordering is suitable.
Oxidation numbers are formal bookkeeping values that must add to the species
charge.
In hydrogen peroxide, take hydrogen as plus one.
Two hydrogen atoms contribute plus two, so the two oxygens together contribute
minus two.
Each oxygen is assigned minus one.
In potassium superoxide, potassium contributes plus one and the oxygen pair
together contributes minus one.
The average oxidation number per oxygen is therefore minus one half.
A fractional average is not a statement that an individual atom contains half
an electron; it describes the bookkeeping of the bonded species.
In oxygen difluoride, each fluorine is minus one.
The oxygen must be plus two so the neutral molecule's total is zero.
Compare these with water, where oxygen is minus two.
The same element can have several assignments because its bonded partners and
connectivity differ.
Apply the sum rule to the actual formula first.
A memorized oxygen value is useful as a common case, but it must yield to a
stated peroxide, superoxide or fluorine containing exception.
Hydrogen bonding can strongly affect boiling without giving the same ordering
for acidity.
Water, ammonia and hydrogen fluoride are familiar hydrogen bonding examples
from different groups.
Compare each with an appropriate set of related hydrides rather than mixing
all
group members into one unexplained ranking.
Down the heavier hydrogen halides, decreasing hydrogen halogen bond strength
supports stronger acidity in the usual dilute aqueous comparison.
Hydrogen fluoride remains the weak member of that elementary acid series
despite fluorine's high electronegativity.
For group sixteen hydrides, acidity generally increases as the central atom
becomes larger and its covalent bond to hydrogen weakens, while water has a
high boiling point because of attractions between molecules.
In group fifteen, ammonia's basicity and hydrogen bonding again require
separate explanations.
A question about thermal stability asks how readily a compound decomposes
under
stated conditions, not how much energy is needed simply to boil it.
Use the property definition, relevant bond or intermolecular interaction and
stated medium to build the comparison.
The practice questions combine these distinctions with oxidation number
calculations.
The molecular forms of nitrogen and white phosphorus illustrate why the first
member of a p block group cannot simply be copied onto its heavier congeners.
Ordinary molecular nitrogen has two atoms joined by a strong triple bond,
represented by one sigma and two pi components.
Molecular white phosphorus instead contains four phosphorus atoms at the
vertices of a tetrahedron.
Each phosphorus is connected to the other three through single bonds.
Counting four vertices times three connections and dividing by two gives six
phosphorus phosphorus bonds, because each edge was counted from both ends.
Twenty valence electrons are available in one molecule containing four
phosphorus atoms.
Six ordinary two electron bonds use twelve, leaving eight electrons as four
lone pairs, one on each atom in the elementary Lewis description.
The tetrahedral drawing describes this molecular allotrope, not every solid
form of phosphorus.
Red and black phosphorus have different extended structures.
Likewise, a larger total bond count in one molecule does not by itself prove
greater chemical stability than another substance; bond strengths, geometry
and
reaction products matter.
Use these structures as examples of catenation and multiple bonding trends,
with the molecular identity and allotrope stated explicitly.
Diborane provides a supporting example of electron deficient bonding in boron
chemistry.
Two boron atoms contribute six valence electrons and six hydrogen atoms
contribute six more, making twelve in total.
Four terminal boron hydrogen bonds use eight electrons in the ordinary two
centre two electron description.
Four electrons remain for two bridging boron hydrogen boron units.
Each bridge is described by a three centre two electron bond, so its electron
pair is shared across three atoms rather than assigned independently to both
drawn boron hydrogen arms.
Two bridge arms therefore do not represent two separate ordinary electron
pairs.
The molecule contains four terminal hydrogens and two bridging hydrogens.
This bookkeeping explains why a conventional drawing with an ordinary two
electron bond on every apparent connection would overcount the available
electrons.
A connectivity projection is useful, but it should not be mistaken for a
complete three dimensional orbital picture.
The example illustrates boron's tendency toward electron deficient structures;
it does not turn every boron compound into the same bonding pattern.
This class uses the compound to explain a group trend, not to prescribe its
preparation or imply that every historical borane reaction is required by the
current syllabus.
Carbon tetrachloride and silicon tetrachloride share a one to four formula
ratio and tetrahedral molecular geometry, but that does not give them
identical
reactions with water.
Carbon tetrachloride resists hydrolysis under ordinary comparison conditions,
whereas silicon tetrachloride reacts readily.
A useful initial accounting representation for silicon replaces four chlorine
atoms by four hydroxyl groups, giving silicon with four hydroxyl groups and
four hydrogen chloride units from four waters.
Subsequent condensation can give hydrated silica; an idealized overall
equation
ending at silicon dioxide uses two waters per silicon tetrachloride and gives
four hydrogen chlorides.
The actual condensed product and hydration depend on conditions.
The contrast reflects differences in the central atoms, bond interactions and
accessible reaction pathways.
It should not be reduced to the claim that an empty d orbital alone explains
every hydrolysis reaction.
Nor should either observation be generalized to all carbon or silicon halides
without checking the compound.
These equations are atom bookkeeping for a supplied chemical comparison, not a
mixing procedure.
Distinguish the initial substitution accounting from a net equation that also
incorporates condensation and water loss.
Oxoacid comparisons need a stated structural family.
For chlorine oxoacids, the usual increasing acid strength trend runs from
hypochlorous acid through chlorous and chloric acids to perchloric acid.
Their formulas contain one, two, three and four oxygen atoms respectively.
Assigning hydrogen plus one and oxygen minus two gives chlorine oxidation
states plus one, plus three, plus five and plus seven.
Additional oxygen helps stabilize the conjugate base through the electronic
effects and delocalization appropriate to each structure.
This is different from comparing hypohalous acids that each contain one
oxygen:
hypochlorous acid is stronger than the corresponding bromine acid, which is
stronger than the iodine acid in the usual comparison.
Here the central atom changes while the oxygen count is held fixed.
Do not combine the two patterns into a rule that ignores molecular structure.
Strong acids can also be levelled by water, so complete ionization or a single
p H measurement at equal nominal concentration is not a universal way to
distinguish their intrinsic strengths.
The useful method is to identify the acid family, write a plausible conjugate
base and then apply the appropriate controlled comparison.
Interhalogen formulas combine different halogen elements and provide useful
oxidation state and shape examples.
In chlorine trifluoride, assign each fluorine minus one, making chlorine plus
three.
The molecule has twenty eight valence electrons.
Three chlorine fluorine bonds use six and the terminal fluorine lone pairs use
eighteen, leaving four electrons as two central lone pairs.
Five electron domains give a trigonal bipyramidal domain arrangement and a T
shaped atomic geometry in the elementary valence shell model.
In bromine pentafluoride, bromine is plus five and the molecule has forty two
valence electrons.
Five bonds use ten and the terminal fluorine lone pairs thirty, leaving one
central lone pair.
Six domains give an octahedral domain arrangement with square pyramidal
molecular shape.
The shape names refer to atomic positions, not to a count of electron pairs
drawn as atoms.
These examples do not assign positive oxidation states to fluorine or prove
that every halogen forms every possible formula.
Electron counting and domain geometry organize the comparison without
requiring
a literal claim that a simple hybrid label completely describes hypervalent
bonding in the real molecule.
The three hydrogens in boric acid do not make it a tribasic acid in its usual
aqueous behaviour.
Boric acid acts as a Lewis acid by accepting an electron pair from hydroxide
to
form tetrahydroxyborate.
One useful net equation writes boric acid plus two waters in equilibrium with
tetrahydroxyborate and hydronium.
Check the inventory: both sides contain one boron, five oxygens and seven
hydrogens, with total charge zero.
In the elementary structural description, the boron environment changes from
three coordinate in boric acid to four coordinate in the borate product.
The familiar description as a weak monobasic acid refers to this aqueous acid
base behaviour, not removal of all three written hydrogens as independent
protons.
Its formal formula alone is insufficient for predicting acid basicity.
The equation describes an equilibrium, so it does not mean every boric acid
molecule converts completely in water.
Other ligands and solution conditions can change speciation.
Use electron pair acceptance, the actual product and charge balance together.
Phosphorus oxoacids illustrate why a molecular formula does not reveal every
acidic hydrogen.
In the usual structural descriptions, hypophosphorous acid has one oxygen
hydrogen group and two phosphorus hydrogen bonds.
Phosphorous acid has two oxygen hydrogen groups and one phosphorus hydrogen
bond.
Phosphoric acid has three oxygen hydrogen groups and no phosphorus hydrogen
bond.
Their ordinary aqueous acid basicities are therefore one, two and three
respectively.
The phosphorus hydrogen bonds are not counted as ordinary ionizable protons in
this comparison.
All three formulas contain three hydrogens, yet their neutralization
capacities
differ.
In a stipulated complete neutralization model, zero point zero one zero zero
mole phosphorous acid consumes zero point zero two zero zero mole hydroxide.
Its phosphorus oxidation number is plus three by hydrogen plus one and oxygen
minus two bookkeeping.
The corresponding oxidation numbers in the other two acids are plus one and
plus five.
Basicity counts the relevant ionizable hydrogens; oxidation number is a
different formal quantity.
Neither count alone determines the numerical acid dissociation constants or
the
actual titration endpoint under unspecified conditions.
Oxygen has molecular allotropes with different structures.
Ozone contains three oxygen atoms and eighteen valence electrons.
Its usual octet Lewis contributors each have one single oxygen oxygen bond and
one double bond, with the central oxygen carrying formal charge plus one and
the singly bonded terminal oxygen minus one.
The two contributors exchange electron placement, not atomic positions.
They describe one bent molecule with equivalent oxygen oxygen links, rather
than a molecule repeatedly switching between two unequal bond arrangements.
Averaging the single and double bond labels gives one point five per link in
this introductory resonance description.
This is an illustrative Lewis bond order, not a complete molecular orbital
calculation.
Ozone is not simply three separate oxygen atoms, and its structure and
reactivity cannot be copied from diatomic oxygen.
The molecular formulas also imply different molar masses: using oxygen
sixteen,
ozone has forty eight grams per mole and dioxygen thirty two.
A comparison of equal mole amounts therefore differs from a comparison of
equal
masses.
Keep molecular identity, electron count and counted amount separate.
Different allotropes contain the same element but organize its atoms
differently.
In diamond, each carbon has four near neighbours in a three dimensional
covalent network.
In graphite, each carbon has three near neighbours within extended layers,
with
delocalized electrons contributing to electrical conduction, especially along
those layers.
Weak interlayer attractions help explain easy sliding, while the strong
bonding
inside a layer remains important.
These descriptions do not make graphite a collection of isolated six carbon
molecules.
Buckminsterfullerene instead consists of discrete sixty carbon cage molecules,
with each carbon connected to three neighbours in the ideal cage.
Counting every cage edge once gives sixty times three divided by two, or
ninety
carbon carbon connections.
Using supplied carbon atomic mass twelve, a mole of these cage molecules has
mass seven hundred twenty grams.
A mole of carbon atoms still has mass twelve grams regardless of allotrope.
Pure ordinary diamond is an electrical insulator, but defects, doping and
measurement conditions can alter actual materials.
Relate properties to connectivity and electronic structure rather than
assigning one universal property to elemental carbon.
The inert pair trend helps organize the increasing importance of lower
oxidation states for some heavier p block elements.
Thallium one, lead two and bismuth three are familiar lower states, while
higher states can act as oxidants in suitable compounds and media.
This is not a rule that every lower state is always the only stable one.
Consider lead dioxide reacting with iodide in a supplied acidic model.
Lead begins in oxidation state plus four and ends as lead two, accepting two
electrons per lead atom.
Two iodide ions lose those two electrons to form one iodine molecule.
Balancing oxygen and hydrogen gives one lead dioxide, four hydrogen ions and
two iodide ions forming one lead two ion, one iodine and two waters.
Thus zero point zero one zero zero mole lead dioxide corresponds theoretically
to the same amount of iodine and twice that amount of iodide.
The compound and medium are essential: an oxidation number alone is not a
complete redox potential.
Treat this as a balanced evidence example supporting a periodic trend, not an
experimental recipe or a claim that every historical p block preparation is
required.
Different reactions of the same nitrogen oxide can involve different kinds of
chemical change.
Nitrogen dioxide has nitrogen in oxidation state plus four.
When two nitrogen dioxide molecules combine to form dinitrogen tetroxide, each
nitrogen remains plus four.
That dimerization changes molecular association but is not a redox reaction by
oxidation number accounting.
In a separate simplified water reaction, two nitrogen dioxide molecules and
one
water give one nitrous acid and one nitric acid.
Nitrogen is plus three in nitrous acid and plus five in nitric acid.
One nitrogen is reduced by one unit while the other is oxidized by one, so
this
net equation represents disproportionation.
It preserves two nitrogen atoms, five oxygen atoms and two hydrogens.
The acid product mixture is not described by merely assigning both nitrogens
the average value plus four and ignoring their individual environments.
Real aqueous nitrogen oxide chemistry can involve further reactions and
conditions, so this equation is a stated introductory model.
Decide whether oxidation states change before classifying a reaction from a
familiar formula or from a colour observation alone.
Sulfur oxoacid formulas illustrate why oxidation state assignments need
connectivity.
In peroxomonosulfuric acid, hydrogen two sulfur oxygen five, one oxygen oxygen
linkage contains two peroxide oxygens.
Assign each of those oxygens minus one and the other three minus two.
With two hydrogens at plus one, sulfur is plus six, not plus eight.
Peroxodisulfuric acid, hydrogen two sulfur two oxygen eight, also contains
one oxygen oxygen linkage.
Its two peroxide oxygens contribute minus two together, while six ordinary
oxygens contribute minus twelve.
The two sulfur atoms therefore contribute plus twelve in total, or plus six
each in the usual symmetric structure.
Disulfuric acid, hydrogen two sulfur two oxygen seven, instead has an oxygen
bridging two sulfur centres and no peroxide linkage.
All seven oxygens have their ordinary minus two assignment, again giving
sulfur
plus six.
Counting two sulfur atoms or an oxygen bridge alone does not establish a
peroxide.
Inspect whether there is an actual oxygen oxygen bond.
These are formal structural and charge ledgers, not directions for preparing
or
handling strongly reactive oxidizing substances.
Noble gas compounds show why a filled shell is not an absolute ban on bonding.
Compare three xenon compounds using formal Lewis electron counting and a
qualitative electron domain model.
Xenon oxyfluoride with one oxygen and four fluorines has forty two valence
electrons.
A drawing with four single xenon fluorine bonds and one double xenon oxygen
bond leaves one central lone pair after terminal octets are completed.
Five bonding domains and one lone pair give an octahedral domain arrangement
and a square pyramidal molecular shape.
Xenon trioxide has twenty six valence electrons.
Three formal double xenon oxygen bonds and terminal oxygen lone pairs leave
one
xenon lone pair, giving three bonding domains and a trigonal pyramidal shape.
Xenon tetroxide has thirty two valence electrons and four bonding domains with
no central lone pair in the corresponding formal drawing, giving tetrahedral
geometry.
A multiple bond counts as one domain for this purpose.
These models do not require asserting literal d orbital expansion as the
bonding mechanism.
Oxidation state is plus six in the first two compounds and plus eight in xenon
tetroxide.
A chemical formula does not guarantee the same structural unit in every phase.
In the molecular gas description, phosphorus pentachloride has five phosphorus
chlorine bonds and trigonal bipyramidal geometry.
Ordinary solid phosphorus pentachloride is instead described by
tetrachlorophosphonium cations and hexachlorophosphate anions.
The cation has four chlorine atoms and tetrahedral geometry, while the anion
has six and octahedral geometry in the elementary electron domain model.
One cation and one anion together contain two phosphorus atoms and ten
chlorines.
That pair therefore corresponds to two empirical phosphorus pentachloride
units, not one.
The cation's valence electron count is five plus four times seven minus one,
or
thirty two.
The anion's is five plus six times seven plus one, or forty eight.
Terminal chlorine lone pairs and the stated bonds account for those electrons
without a central lone pair in either ion.
Phosphorus oxidation state remains plus five in both charged species; overall
ion charge is not its oxidation state.
This phase comparison does not claim that every hot vapour remains entirely
undissociated or that every phosphorus halide has the same solid structure.
Disproportionation puts atoms of the same starting element into both lower and
higher oxidation states.
In the usual cold dilute alkali comparison, chlorine gives chloride and
hypochlorite, with chlorine oxidation numbers minus one and plus one.
One chlorine molecule and two hydroxides form one of each ion and one water.
In the familiar hot concentrated alkali comparison, the idealized overall
products are chloride and chlorate.
Chlorate has chlorine plus five, so one chlorine atom losing five electrons
must be balanced by five chlorine atoms each gaining one.
The net equation therefore uses three chlorine molecules and six hydroxides to
form five chlorides, one chlorate and three waters.
Five sixths of the chlorine atoms are reduced and one sixth oxidized in this
second ledger.
For zero point zero three zero zero mole chlorine completely following that
stipulated endpoint, chlorate amount is zero point zero one zero zero mole and
chloride zero point zero five zero zero mole.
These are alternative condition dependent overall comparisons, not two
identical product ratios.
The equations balance atoms and charge but do not specify an elementary
mechanism, a universal reaction rate or an experimental preparation procedure.
Boron trihalides can accept a lone pair from a Lewis base, but ranking them
requires a specified comparison.
Let the same donor L form one to one adducts with boron trifluoride,
trichloride and tribromide in a supplied matched state model.
Their illustrative formation enthalpies are minus eighty, minus one hundred
and
minus one hundred fifteen kilojoules per mole adduct.
Tribromide formation is most exothermic in this dataset.
The planar three coordinate boron parent becomes approximately four coordinate
in the adduct, so binding includes the energy needed to deform the parent as
well as the new donor acceptor interaction.
Electron donation within the parent molecule can influence its bonding, but
one
electronegativity arrow or a simple octet count does not account for all these
energy terms.
The familiar acidity ordering toward suitable strong donors need not be an
invariant ranking toward every weak donor or in every solvent.
Nor do the supplied enthalpies alone determine equilibrium constants: Gibbs
energy also includes entropy at the stated temperature.
These original numbers illustrate matched data interpretation, not a set of
measured universal constants or proof that an acid base equilibrium is a redox
reaction.
Silicate formulas can be understood by counting shared oxygen corners rather
than treating every silicon oxygen unit as an isolated molecule.
In the supplied ideal model, every silicon is surrounded by four oxygens, and
a
bridging oxygen belongs to two silicon centres.
If k corners per tetrahedron are shared, the oxygen count per silicon is four
minus k over two.
With silicon plus four and oxygen minus two, net charge per silicon formula
unit is k minus four.
An isolated tetrahedron, with no shared corners, is silicon oxygen four
carrying charge minus four.
A pair sharing one corner has two silicons and seven oxygens, with total
charge
minus six.
An ideal infinite chain with two shared corners per tetrahedron has repeating
ratio silicon oxygen three and charge minus two per silicon.
A fully corner shared pure silica framework has ratio silicon oxygen two and
zero net formal charge.
Finite chain ends, hydroxyl groups, aluminium substitution and counterions
require additional bookkeeping, so these simple ratios do not describe every
mineral without modification.
A shared silicon oxygen silicon bridge is not an oxygen oxygen peroxide bond.
The counting graph identifies connectivity; it does not make the actual
tetrahedra planar.
Similar halide names do not imply identical hydrolysis products.
In the selected complete hydrolysis comparison, phosphorus trichloride gives
phosphorous acid and three hydrogen chloride units, using three waters per
phosphorus.
Phosphorus pentachloride gives phosphoric acid and five hydrogen chloride
units, using four waters per phosphorus.
Phosphorus stays at oxidation state plus three in the first reaction and plus
five in the second, so neither net hydrolysis is itself a phosphorus redox
change.
The familiar structures of the acid products also differ.
Phosphorous acid has two oxygen hydrogen groups and one phosphorus hydrogen
bond, giving two ordinarily ionizable protons in this comparison.
Phosphoric acid has three oxygen hydrogen groups and is triprotic.
Counting the three hydrogens in each formula without checking connectivity
would give the wrong basicity for phosphorous acid.
Limited water can give different intermediate endpoints for the pentachloride,
so the complete hydrolysis equations must not be applied indiscriminately.
These selected compound balances support structural comparisons.
They are conceptual equations, not handling instructions or a claim that every
historical preparation belongs to the current trend focused syllabus.
An intermediate oxidation state can participate in different redox roles
depending on the reaction partner.
Sulfur in sulfur dioxide is plus four.
When sulfur dioxide is oxidized to sulfate, sulfur becomes plus six and loses
two electrons per sulfur atom.
In a supplied aqueous bromine comparison, the balanced net equation contains
one sulfur dioxide, one bromine molecule and two waters, forming sulfate, four
hydrogen ions and two bromides.
Sulfur dioxide acts as the reducing agent because it is oxidized.
Contrast the selected reaction with hydrogen sulfide: one sulfur dioxide plus
two hydrogen sulfide molecules gives three elemental sulfur atoms and two
waters.
Sulfur in sulfur dioxide falls from plus four to zero, accepting four
electrons, while each sulfide sulfur rises from minus two to zero and loses
two.
Sulfur dioxide is the oxidizing agent in that comparison.
The two starting sulfur oxidation states converge to an intermediate state,
which is comproportionation rather than disproportionation.
An oxidation number identifies possible electron changes, but does not by
itself establish every reaction's feasibility or rate.
Always name the partner and the stated products.
Hydrogen peroxide illustrates why a reagent should not receive one universal
redox label.
Each peroxide oxygen has oxidation number minus one.
In an acidic reduction half reaction, one peroxide molecule accepts two
electrons and two hydrogen ions to form two waters.
Its oxygen reaches minus two, so peroxide acts as an oxidizing agent when
paired with iodide oxidation.
The net equation gives one iodine molecule and two waters from one peroxide,
two iodides and two hydrogen ions.
Peroxide can instead lose two electrons per molecule and form oxygen gas, with
oxygen oxidation number zero.
Against acidic permanganate it therefore acts as a reducing agent.
Combining the electron counts gives two permanganates, five peroxides and six
hydrogen ions forming two manganese two ions, five oxygen molecules and eight
waters.
One hundredth mole of peroxide would correspond ideally to four thousandths
mole permanganate and one hundredth mole oxygen for this specified complete
reaction.
These are theoretical stoichiometric amounts, not claims about arbitrary
mixtures or decomposition yields.
Track the peroxide oxygen's destination and the partner half reaction before
assigning its role.
A balanced halogen redox equation is needed before using a limiting reagent
ratio.
In the supplied acidic iodate iodide reaction, iodine at plus five in iodate
and iodine at minus one in iodide both end at zero in molecular iodine.
One iodate iodine accepts five electrons.
Five iodide iodines each lose one electron, giving six iodine atoms in three
iodine molecules.
Balancing oxygen and hydrogen adds six hydrogen ions on the left and three
waters on the right.
This is comproportionation of two oxidation states of the same element.
Suppose a stipulated complete reaction starts with two millimoles of iodate,
eight millimoles of iodide and sufficient acid.
Compare two millimoles of iodate with eight divided by five, or one point six
millimoles of reaction extent supported by iodide.
Iodide limits the extent.
The theoretical iodine product is three times one point six, giving four point
eight millimoles, while zero point four millimole iodate remains.
Do not equate one iodate molecule to one iodine molecule.
Solution speciation and competing reactions require additional information
